How Did One Woman Measure the Universe?

Episode 118 of a daily journey through the universe. ⭐
For International Women's Day: Henrietta Swan Leavitt, a Harvard 'computer' paid cents an hour, discovered in 1908–1912 that Cepheid stars' blinking reveals their true brightness, the measuring tape Edwin Hubble used in 1923 to prove Andromeda is another galaxy.

segments.text: How do you measure the universe? One woman figured it out, using blinking stars.
A century ago, Henrietta Swan Leavitt worked at Harvard as a computer. A person who studied photos of the sky by hand, for a few cents an hour.
segments.headline: Harvard's human computers

segments.text: She studied stars that blink, getting brighter and dimmer over days. They're called Cepheids.
segments.headline: Blinking stars

segments.text: In the Small Magellanic Cloud, she noticed something amazing. The slower a Cepheid blinks, the brighter it really is.
segments.headline: Her big discovery

segments.text: She published the rule in nineteen twelve. Now, if you time a Cepheid's blinking, you know its true brightness.
Compare that to how bright it looks from Earth, and you can work out how far away it is. A cosmic measuring tape.
In nineteen twenty-three, Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid in the Andromeda nebula, and measured its distance.
segments.headline: Hubble finds V1

segments.text: Andromeda was far outside the Milky Way. It was a whole other galaxy. The universe suddenly became huge.
segments.headline: A whole other galaxy

segments.text: Leavitt died in nineteen twenty-one, before seeing what her discovery led to. Astronomers still use her law today.
segments.headline: Still used today
